name: Whitening gel trays
lead: Whitening gel trays are flexible plastic trays that hold a peroxide-based bleaching gel against the teeth, usually for a period of minutes to hours or overnight. They are available as custom-fitted trays made by a dentist from impressions or digital scans, and as over-the-counter boil-and-bite or prefilled versions. The active ingredient is hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide, which releases hydrogen peroxide on contact with water. [1][2]

The hydrogen peroxide that is released diffuses into the tooth and breaks down pigmented organic molecules into smaller, less strongly coloured fragments, which makes the tooth reflect more light and appear whiter. [1] Because the tray keeps gel in contact with the tooth surfaces and, when well fitted, away from the gums, tray-based bleaching is one of the standard take-home options in dentistry. [1][3]

Clinical trials of tray bleaching with carbamide peroxide and hydrogen peroxide report measurable colour change on spectrophotometers, and the main adverse effects are tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, which are generally reported as temporary. [4][5][6] A scoping review of over-the-counter bleaching products noted that evidence for whitening strips comes mostly from clinical trials, whereas evidence for over-the-counter trays comes mainly from laboratory studies. [7] In looksmaxxing and fitness forums, trays are usually discussed as a cheaper alternative to strips or in-office treatment, often with a dentist-made custom tray as the preferred version. [8][9]
infobox: Tooth-bleaching delivery device (tray plus peroxide gel)
Carbamide peroxide or hydrogen peroxide gel [1]
About 2 hours daily for 3 weeks (22% carbamide peroxide); overnight for 4 weeks (10% carbamide peroxide) [10][11]

paras: A whitening tray is a thin, shaped reservoir of soft plastic that is loaded with gel and seated over the upper and/or lower teeth. Wikipedia lists tray-based whitening among the at-home options alongside strips, gels painted on with a brush, rinses and whitening toothpastes, and notes that trays are available both over the counter and through dental professionals. [1]

Custom trays are vacuum-formed on a cast or printed from an intraoral scan so that they match the patient's arch; dentists may add small reservoirs over the front surfaces of teeth to hold more gel. A laboratory study of trays with and without reservoirs examined colour change in mounted teeth and also compared time and cost. [13] Boil-and-bite trays are softened in hot water and moulded by the user, and prefilled disposable trays come already loaded with gel. A randomized trial used a prefilled tray with 6% hydrogen peroxide for the at-home portion of a combined protocol. [14]

Gel strength differs by product and by whether the tray is professionally supplied. Grokipedia describes dentist-supervised take-home trays as using moderate carbamide peroxide concentrations of roughly 10 to 38 percent, worn for several hours a day over one to four weeks, while over-the-counter products use lower concentrations; Grokipedia is an AI-generated source and its figures are given here only as a general description. [2] Trials in the published literature have used, for example, 22% carbamide peroxide for two hours daily and 10% carbamide peroxide overnight. [10][11]

Carbamide peroxide breaks down into hydrogen peroxide and urea; hydrogen peroxide then acts as an oxidising agent that generates unstable free radicals within the spaces of the enamel and dentine, attaching to organic pigment molecules and splitting them into smaller components that absorb less light. [1] Wikipedia notes that the end point depends on the time of exposure and the concentration of the bleaching compound. [1]

The design rationale for trays is that a sealed reservoir allows longer, lower-concentration exposure than a brief high-concentration application, and keeps gel off the soft tissue. [1][3] Wikipedia also records that poorly fitting trays are among the commonest reasons for chemical burns of the gums, and that custom-made trays can reduce this by limiting leakage onto the mucosa. [1]
Evidence for tray bleaching comes from randomized trials, systematic reviews and laboratory studies; the points below summarise what specific studies report.

A systematic review and meta-analysis compared tray-delivered carbamide peroxide with tray-delivered hydrogen peroxide for at-home bleaching. [15] A Cochrane review examined home-based chemically induced whitening of teeth in adults. [16] An umbrella review compared in-office and at-home bleaching techniques for efficacy and post-operative sensitivity. [17]

A 2024 scoping review of 88 studies of over-the-counter bleaching products found that most clinical evidence concerned whitening strips, which were reported to improve tooth colour, while the effectiveness of toothpastes, rinses and whitening trays was mainly supported by laboratory studies; tooth sensitivity and gum irritation were the main adverse effects across products. [7]

In a 50-participant randomized trial, volunteers wore trays containing 22% carbamide peroxide for two hours a day for 21 days; the study tested whether photobiomodulation therapy and a remineralising paste could reduce sensitivity without reducing shade change. Participants given placebo had the largest increase in sensitivity during bleaching. [10]

In a randomized trial of 66 participants, an in-office 35% hydrogen peroxide treatment was combined with a prefilled at-home tray containing 6% hydrogen peroxide used between office visits. Colour change rose with the number of sessions in all groups, the group using the home tray ten times showed significantly greater colour change than the in-office-only group at the third session, and sensitivity was higher up to 24 hours after treatment. [14] A follow-up report on the same participants tracked colour stability for up to two years and found that colour change gradually decreased in all groups and that stability differed between protocols. [18]

A split-mouth randomized trial of 30 participants using 10% carbamide peroxide for two weeks on either the upper or lower arch found greater colour change on the bleached arch, and also found that vacuum-formed orthodontic retainers worn during bleaching had lower tensile strength, greater hardness and greater internal roughness than on the unbleached arch. [19]

In a 40-person single-blind randomized trial of nightguard vital bleaching in people with pre-existing sensitivity, participants first wore custom trays with no gel to assess sensitivity caused by the tray alone and were then randomized to a desensitizing agent or placebo applied in the tray before whitening. [20]

A 52-patient study of overnight bleaching with 10% carbamide peroxide in trays for four weeks used standardized photographs to track colour change weekly and at four months, and a five-year follow-up of digital colour evaluation has been published. [21][22]

An in situ study examined the effect of 10% and 15% carbamide peroxide on the fracture toughness of human dentine, a question prompted by laboratory reports of effects on hard tissues. [23] A study of whitening under orthodontic brackets measured colour change in enamel and dentine with specially designed preloaded trays. [24] A 2024 toxicology paper estimated per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) exposure from leave-in dental products, including whitening trays and night guards, in a convenience sample. [25]

Wikipedia lists tooth sensitivity, gum irritation and uneven results among the common effects of whitening, and reports that sensitivity after in-office hydrogen peroxide treatment affects a majority of recipients; it also states that home-based bleaching following manufacturer instructions tends to cause less sensitivity than in-office bleaching. [1] Grokipedia gives a range of 8 to 66 percent for transient sensitivity in users. [2]

Wikipedia describes concentrations of 10% hydrogen peroxide or more as capable of irritating or damaging mucous membranes if they contact unprotected tissue. [1] The 2024 scoping review likewise names sensitivity and gingival irritation as the main adverse effects of over-the-counter bleaching. [7] Trials of sensitivity management have tested desensitising agents and photobiomodulation as add-ons. [10][20]

Groups listed by Wikipedia as needing caution include people with existing sensitive teeth, cracked or exposed dentine, gum recession, defective restorations, peroxide allergy, and people who are pregnant or breastfeeding; it also notes that bleaching does not change the colour of crowns, veneers or fillings, which can produce a shade mismatch. [1]

Fitness and self-improvement forums have discussed trays for many years. Posters in T Nation threads from the mid-2000s describe the dentist route as a custom-moulded tray with a supplied gel, warn that it can make teeth more sensitive and irritate the gums, and mention strips as the alternative; one poster asked whether a roughly $250 orthodontist-supplied system was worth the price. [26][27] Another thread describes mail-order custom trays made from a home impression kit. [28] A 2010 thread in the same forum recommends home whitening as part of a list of grooming steps to improve first impressions. [29] A Reddit thread asking for the best teeth whitening product to buy illustrates the continuing consumer interest. [30]

Discussion typically compares four routes: strips, custom dentist trays, over-the-counter boil-and-bite trays and in-office bleaching, with custom trays described by proponents as giving more even coverage and as lasting through repeated top-up use. Research reports on this point are mixed: the umbrella review cited above compares office and home approaches, and the scoping review notes that clinical evidence for over-the-counter trays is sparser than for strips. [7][17]

Wikipedia advises that a dental examination before whitening lets a clinician identify decay, defective restorations and sensitivity risks, and that clinicians typically remove surface stain first. [1] Dental sources distinguish custom-fitted trays, which seal against the gum margin, from stock or boil-and-bite trays that may let gel leak, and Wikipedia attributes burns most often to poorly fitting trays. [1] Gel concentration, wear time and the presence of reservoirs vary across products and are the main parameters studied in trials. [10][13]

timeline.event: Randomized trial of a desensitizing agent during nightguard vital bleaching in people prone to sensitivity is published. [20]
In situ study of 10% and 15% carbamide peroxide and dentine fracture toughness is published. [23]
Systematic review and meta-analysis compares tray carbamide and hydrogen peroxide for at-home bleaching. [15]
Cochrane review of home-based bleaching of adult teeth is published. [16]
Scoping review of 88 studies of over-the-counter bleaching products is published. [7]
Two-year follow-up of combined in-office and prefilled-tray bleaching is published. [18]

lore.intro: Trays are discussed in forums mainly as the middle option between drugstore strips and in-office bleaching, with custom dentist trays often described as the best value and sensitivity as the usual complaint. [26][27][28]

claims.claim: Custom trays give more even whitening than strips.
claims.believers: Posters describe a moulded tray as covering every tooth surface and holding gel in place, in contrast to strips that cover the front of the teeth only. [26][28]
claims.experts: A scoping review found that clinical evidence for over-the-counter trays is thinner than for strips, whose effectiveness is supported by clinical trials. [7] Reviews compare tray carbamide and hydrogen peroxide systems and home with office approaches. [15][17]

claims.claim: A dentist-made tray is worth the higher price over over-the-counter versions.
claims.believers: Forum users ask whether a roughly $250 orthodontist-supplied system is worth it and describe custom molds as the standard dentist method. [27][31]
claims.experts: Wikipedia attributes chemical burns most often to poorly fitting trays and says custom-made trays reduce leakage onto the gums. [1] No trial in the material reviewed compared custom and over-the-counter trays head to head.

claims.claim: Whitening trays make teeth sensitive and irritate gums.
claims.believers: T Nation posters describe sensitivity and gum irritation from peroxide gel as expected effects. [26]
claims.experts: Trials and reviews list sensitivity and gingival irritation as the main adverse effects, and several trials test desensitising agents. [7][10][20]

claims.claim: Bleaching trays are harmless to enamel and other dental materials.
claims.believers: Users commonly treat trays as a routine cosmetic step comparable to brushing and rarely mention structural effects.
claims.experts: An in situ study examined dentine fracture toughness under 10% and 15% carbamide peroxide, and a split-mouth trial found changes in the mechanical properties of orthodontic vacuum-formed retainers worn with bleaching. [19][23]

claims.claim: Whitening results from trays are lasting.
claims.believers: Site rating and many posts describe trays as a durable cosmetic improvement that can be topped up.
claims.experts: A two-year trial of combined protocols reported that colour change gradually decreased over time in all groups. [18] Wikipedia notes that colour can rebound and that diet affects results. [1]
